senses.gloss:
patnīśālā
(‘a shed for the wife’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices involved the construction of large (temporary) sheds meant for various purposes. One such shed with the bamboo beams protruding towards the east was called ‘prācīnavaṁśa’.
In this shed a small part was set apart and screened off where the patnī or the wife of the yajamāna (the sacrificer) was supposed to stay during the perfor-mance of the प्रवर्ग्य, a minor rite in a सोमयाग, which she was not supposed to see. Hence the name.

pativratā
(‘[a woman] deeply devoted to her husband’)
------------------------------------------
Conjugal felicity depends to a very great extent on mutual trust and concern, between the husband and the wife. Though this was stressed as the general rule, the onus was much more on woman than on man.
Perhaps to help the wife by moral support and encouragement, the virtue of being a pativratā—a chaste wife—was eulogised highly in the scriptures, especially in the धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस्.
Single-minded devotion and service to her husband as also the rigid observance of all the rules prescribed for her—voluntarily and willingly—made her a पतिव्रता.
The definition of a पतिव्रता given by बृहस्पति and quoted by other authors of धर्मशास्त्रस्, gives us, perhaps, the best idea of that ideal: ‘She is distressed when her husband is distressed and is delighted when he is delighted. She becomes emaciated and wears soiled clothes when her husband goes out on a journey. And, she dies when her husband dies!’
The following women are held before the Hindu society as the ideal pativratās fit to be emulated: सीता, सावित्री, दमयन्ती, अनसूया and द्रौपदी.
Other lists include सती, पार्वती, अरुन्धती and Śāṇḍili.
The Mahābhārata (Vanaparva chs. 205-206) describes how a devoted wife attained everything including yogic powers, just by serving her husband.
The story of सावित्री who succeeded in bringing her husband back from the clutches of यम (the god of death) is too well-known to be repeated (vide Vanaparva of Mahābhārata, chs. 293-299).

Pātāla
(‘[the evildoers] fall [into this]’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् describe fourteen worlds. Out of these, six are higher worlds above this earth (= भूलोक). Seven are below. They are: अतल, वितल, सुतल, तलातल, महातल, रसातल and पाताल.
According to this list, पाताल is the nethermost world. It is the abode of serpents. The serpent-chiefs who live here are: Aśvadhara, Devadatta, Dhanañjaya, धृतराष्ट्र, Gulika, Kambala, Mahā-śikha, शङ्ख, Śaṅkhacūḍa, Śveta and वासुकि.
At the base of the पाताल is a place separated from the rest where lives अनन्त or आदिशेष or Śeṣanāga. He is said to be carrying all the worlds on his thousand hoods.
All the eleven great serpents mentioned above have brilliant gems on their hoods, the light emanating from which illuminates the netherworld.
According to the Mahābhārata (vide Udyogaparva 99) पाताल is inhabited by दैत्यस् (demons), govratis (persons of great austerity) and maharṣis (great sages) as also the four elephant kings (Airāvaṇa, वामन, Kumuda and Añjana) who are guarding the quarters.
As per the long description given in the Vyāsabhāṣya on the Yogasūtras (3.26) the पाताल-लोक has oceans and mountains. All types of beings like असुरस्, गन्धर्वस्, किम्पुरुषस्, yakṣas and राक्षसस् as also various kinds of disembodied spirits (bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, brahmarākṣasas and so on) live here.

Patañjali
------------------------------------------
‘Patañjali’ is a great name in Sanskrit literature, both in its secular and the sacred aspects.
He is generally assigned to the 2nd century B. C.. He was the son of Goṇikā. His ड़थेर्’s name is not known. He had his एदुचतिओन् at तक्षशिला (Taxila, now in Pakistan). He was a familiar figure in the countries called Vāhīka and गान्धार.
The word ‘Patañjali’ means ‘one who fell into the cupped hand’. When a sage of Gonarda (a country?) was praying to the Sun-god with water in his cupped-hands (= añjali) a little baby fell ‘from the आकाश’ (or sky) into it. He gave that baby-boy to a woman called Goṇikā (who had no children) to be brought up.
According to another version, Goṇikā, the daughter of a sage, was offering अर्घ्य (sacred water in hand, joined as a cup) to सूर्य (Sun-god) with the specific desire of getting a son when a baby-boy fell into her hands. This baby-boy was none other than आदिशेष, the king of serpents and the bed of Lord विष्णु!
Hindu tradition ascribes three works to पतञ्जलि. He wrote them to help people to cleanse the impurities of their body, speech and मिन्द्. The first one is a work on the आयुर्वेद which has not been traced till now. (Some scholars opine that the Carakasaṁhitā is actually his work, though others disagree.) The second one is his Mahābhāṣya on the sūtras of पाणिनि, a well-known work of Sanskrit grammar, called Aṣṭādhyāyī. The last is the Yoga-sūtras.
The Mahābhāṣya is in 85 āhnikas or sections. Its diction is most elegant and has been considered as a model for Sanskrit prose. Apart from the explanations of the sūtras of पाणिनि, this commentary contains a lot of additional information and discussions.
Though this Mahābhāṣya has several commentaries, the Pradīpa of Kaiyaṭa (circa 5th cent. A. D.) is the most well-known.
The Yogasūtras is the basic text for योग philosophy and practice of योग. It has several commentaries of which the Bhāṣya of व्यास (A. D. 600) and the Tattvavaiśāradī of वाचस्पति (A. D. 850) on this Bhāṣya are the best-known.
See also AṢṬĀDHYĀYĪ and PĀṆINI.

patitasāvitrīka
(‘[one who has] fallen [from the sacrament of being taught the] सावित्री [mantra]’)
------------------------------------------
In the ancient days, for a द्विज (the ‘twice-born’ class, viz., a ब्राह्मण, a क्षत्त्रिय and a वैश्य), to be initiated into the सावित्री or the गायत्री मन्त्र was considered as an absolute necessity. This initiation gave him the right to study the वेदस्, perform वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् and attain some status in the society.
Sometimes, due to some unknown or extraordinary reasons, a person might have missed this sacrament even after the proper or the permitted age is past (this age being 8 to 16 years in the case of ब्राह्मणस् 11 to 22 years for kṣattriyas and 12 to 24 for vaiśyas).
Such persons came to be known as ‘patitasāvitrīkas’. They were deprived of the right to Vedic studies and were treated almost as outcastes.
In case such persons wanted the उपनयन sacrament (along with the teaching of the सावित्रीमन्त्र) to be performed, they had to undergo some prāyaścittas or expiations.
Different writers of धर्मशास्त्रस् prescribed different kinds of expiations such as: undergoing the disciplines of ब्रह्मचर्य or studenthood for two months after which his उपनयन could be performed; or, the performance of उद्दालकव्रत (subsisting on barley gruel for two months and so on) (See UDDĀLAKA-VRATA for details.); or, three प्राजापत्य penances (See PRĀJĀPATYA.) and so on.
In case the ड़थेर्, or ड़थेर् and grandfather, of the पतितसावित्रीक were also fallen ones (in this sense), the penances were harsher.

pātaka
(‘that which takes one down [to nether regions like हेल्ल्]’)
------------------------------------------
Belief in a Supernatural Being or Power—generally called ‘God’—is ingrained in the human psyche. The words of a scripture and/or of the men of God, are considered as sacrosanct and hence, inviolable. Not following them or going against them has always been regarded as a sin resulting in grave consequences.
The Hindu scriptures have designated such sins by various names such as: āgas, aghaḥ, aṁhas, durita, duṣkṛta, enas, पाप, pāpman, पातक, vṛjina and so on.
The concept of पातक or sin is as old as the Ṛgveda (1.17.1; 8.47.2) wherein prayers have been offered to the deities like आदित्य, मित्र and वरुण for redemption.
The question as to what causes sin and how it is committed has been discussed in the धर्मशास्त्रस्. The Gītā (16.21) declares that काम (lust), krodha (anger) and लोभ (greed) born out of the rajoguṇa (in the मिन्द्) (See GUṆA for details.) are responsible for a person to perpetrate evil deeds, thereby accumulating sins.
Some of the earliest धर्मशास्त्रस् (like those of गौतम, याज्ञवल्क्य and मनु) list the following lapses and misdeeds as leading to sins: doing यज्ञ (sacrifice) for an unworthy person, eating forbidden ड़ोओद्, speaking untruth, neglect of prescribed duties, committing deeds declared as evil by the śāstras or holy books and lack of self control.
In course of time, the list was enlarged to include many more items.
All the sins will result in physical and psychological suffering. Graphic des-criptions of hells given in the पुराणस् seem to be an attempt at dissuading human beings from committing sins.
Sins have been classified in several ways. The most common classification is into three groups: महापातकस् or atipātakas (most heinous or mortal sins); upapātakas (minor sins, venial sins) and prakīrṇa or prāsaṅgika (miscellaneous, incidental).
Under the first category are given the following sins: prohibited sexual relations like incest; murdering; drinking liquor; theft; association with those who have committed these sins; reviling the वेदस्; giving false evidence to harm others and so on.
The second category includes such minor sins as: forsaking the sacred fires; offending the गुरु; becoming an atheist; minor thefts; accepting remuneration for teaching the वेदस्; usury and so on.
It is interesting to note that cutting of big trees for fuel was also included in the latter list!
Sins omitted from these two groups and considered as very minor, are relegated to the third or the last group.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस् have also specified the prāyaścittas (expi-ations) or the various means of reducing the consequences of these sins. They are: pāpanivedana (confession); paścāttāpa (repentance); प्राणायाम (restraint of breath); तपस् (austerity); होम (sacrifice into a duly consecrated fire); जप (repetition of Vedic passages as prayers); दान (giving gifts); उपवास (fasting); and तीर्थयात्रा (pilgrimage).
Pāpanivedana should be done before God or the sacred fire or the परिषद् (an assembly of learned persons of unblemished character).
This should be followed by paścāttāpa and a firm resolve, not to repeat the sin.
Prāṇāyāma burns up the impurities of the मिन्द् and purifies it. The number should be as prescribed in the śāstras or by the परिषद्.
Tapas has many aspects such as ड़स्तिन्ग् (partial or full), celibacy, truthfulness, bathing thrice a day, wearing of wet clothes until they dry up (on the body), sleeping on the ground, not injuring others, serving the preceptor and so on. The period may extend from one month up to 12 months, depending on the nature of the sin.
As regards the होम, it is the कूष्माण्डहोम, using the mantras of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (2.3-6), that is normally prescribed. This होम has been specially recommended for the expiation of sins.
Gaṇahoma and Gāyatrīhoma are also sometimes prescribed.
These are preceded by a दीक्षा (initi-ation) wherein a set of rules and discipline such as abstaining from meat, sex and falsehood, sleeping on the ground, subsisting on milk and so on, are also to be observed strictly. These homas please the deities for whom they are done. They (the deities) forgive the sins and also grant boons.
Japa can be with the Vedic or the Āgamic mantras. Certain passages like the Aghamarṣaṇasūkta and the Puruṣa-sūkta or the sāmans like Rājata and Rauhiṇeya as also some Upaniṣadic passages are prescribed in the first group. Well-known mantras like the गायत्री, the पञ्चाक्षरी and the अष्टाक्षरी are recommended in the second group. (Rāmamantra often called the तारकमन्त्र also finds an important place.) For that matter, any मन्त्र of any deity, duly received from a competent गुरु, can be used for expiation.
For दान or giving gifts, many things are mentioned such as gold, cow, clothes, horse, land, ड़ोओद् etc. Gifts may be offered to temples and religious institutions also.
During उपवास or ड़स्तिन्ग्, which can be total or partial, the sinner is advised to avoid luxury articles, sleeping in daytime and sex completely.
Tīrthayātrā or पिल्ग्रिमगे should be undertaken to well-known and highly recommended places like काशी, Badarī, Kedāra and रामेश्वरम्.
Association with a saint and serving him is also an aspect of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Ultimately, it can safely be declared that the following disciplines are the best means of overcoming or attenuating the evil effects of sin on one’s life: sincere repentance, resolving not to repeat the sinful deeds, repetition of God’s name, earnest prayer and the company of holy persons.
